headline: Connecticut computer science enrollment falls as schools face new AI mandate
dek: About 3,000 fewer Connecticut students took computer science courses than in 2022-23, even as a new state law expands the role of computer science and artificial intelligence in education.
body: Connecticut’s computer science enrollment has fallen for a third consecutive year, creating a policy mismatch as the state asks schools to prepare students for an economy increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence. About 3,000 fewer students were taking computer science courses in 2025-26 than in the 2022-23 school year, according to data reviewed by [CT Insider](https://www.stamfordadvocate.com/news/education/article/connecticut-computer-science-enrollment-decline-22473672.php). The decline amounted to 1.5 percentage points over that period.

The figures come from the Connecticut State Department of Education’s EdSight computer science dashboard, the state’s public system for tracking course offerings and enrollment by school, district and statewide category. The [dashboard](https://public-edsight.ct.gov/instruction/computer-science-dashboard) makes the underlying reports available for export, but enrollment totals are not the same thing as the number of students who want to work in technology. A student may take a course without pursuing a related career, while another may study coding through a technical program or outside school and not appear in the specific measure.

The recent drop also is not spread evenly across course types. CT Insider reported that traditional offerings such as coding and robotics experienced the largest declines, while more interdisciplinary computer science classes posted a modest increase in the last school year. That distinction matters because a school can maintain some computer-related instruction while losing the dedicated courses that give students sustained practice with programming, computational problem-solving and technical projects.

The numbers point to several possible pressures rather than one confirmed cause. John Tusch, president of the Connecticut chapter of the Computer Science Teachers Association and a longtime educator, told CT Insider that graduation requirements, school budgets and a shortage of qualified teachers can all compete with computer science for classroom space. He also said interest dipped after generative AI became widely visible but later began to recover. The state data show what happened to enrollment; they do not establish how much of the change came from AI, staffing, scheduling or local budget decisions.

District resources appear to be part of the story. In the comparison reported by CT Insider, 20 of the state’s highest-funded districts saw computer science participation fall 2.3 percentage points, or about 550 students, between 2023-24 and 2025-26. The 20 lowest-funded districts showed virtually no change over that same period. A separate comparison by free- and reduced-price lunch status found a 3.5-point decline in higher-income districts and a 2.2-point decline in lower-income districts. Those groupings describe patterns, not a verdict on any particular district or the quality of its programs.

Connecticut is responding with a stronger policy commitment at the same time participation is weakening. Gov. Ned Lamont announced in June that he had signed [Public Act 26-15](https://portal.ct.gov/governor/news/press-releases/2026/06-2026/governor-lamont-signs-legislation-establishing-youth-online-safety-protections), a broad law that includes initiatives for AI literacy, workforce training and a statewide AI Academy. The legislation also expands the state’s computer science education and workforce-development account, according to the [Connecticut General Assembly’s 2026 bill materials](https://www.cga.ct.gov/2026/amd/S/pdf/2026SB-00005-R00SA-AMD.pdf). The policy direction is clear, but the law cannot by itself supply teachers, add sections to a master schedule or persuade students to enroll.

That implementation gap is especially important for Connecticut districts because access to a course depends on local capacity. A district needs an available teacher, appropriate equipment and enough student demand to run a class without displacing another graduation or career requirement. The state Department of Education says computer science can count within the STEM credit pathway and maintains standards and implementation resources, but those statewide tools leave day-to-day scheduling and staffing decisions with local schools.

The next useful measure will be whether the new policy changes enrollment in the 2026-27 school year and whether growth reaches the traditional programming courses that declined most. State officials and districts will also need to distinguish computer science from general technology use: learning to operate an AI tool is not the same as understanding algorithms, data, software design or the limits of an automated answer. For now, the verified picture is a Connecticut system trying to expand the subject’s importance while fewer students are taking the courses that have historically defined it.
